To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) conservation managers need to determine what timeframe to target, (2) the timeframe should be based on the species’ evolutionary time frame, (3) the timeframe is not necessarily the timeframe that the species evolved, (4) the timeframe is based on a species’ evolutionary time scale (i.e. generation time) and the timeframe that humans have altered the landscape, and (5) managers need to be able to predict how climate change will alter the species’ evolutionary envelope and plan accordingly
we need to have a clear target to manage for and that this target should be the past, present, and future.
conservation managers should aim to restore the biodiversity of the past, present, and future.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing the science and tools for conservation management in the Anthropocene.
the future of biodiversity.
the conservation of biodiversity in the past, present, and future.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
conservation should be focused on the past, present, and future of the environment.
conservation managers should manage for a future in which biodiversity is conserved and restored to the levels that existed in the past.
we should aim to restore ecosystems and species to a state that they have been in the past, but we must do so in the context of the future.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a framework to help guide conservation management for the past (historical), present and future (predictive) and have demonstrated how it can work using a case study of the endangered Australian lungfish (Neoceratodus forsteri).
conservation management is a dynamic, ever-changing field that requires managers to be flexible and adaptable to the ever-changing environment.
we are trying to understand the past and present, to inform the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
conservation management should be based on a long-term timeframe of 1000 years.
we need a new paradigm for conservation that is based upon a long-term timeframe.
we should be aiming for a more dynamic and adaptive approach to conservation that incorporates the best science available, rather than the status quo.
